# Analytic Standards

> Copy of [Analytic Standards](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes/blob/main/docs/analytic-standards.md) from [Intelligence Field Notes](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes) 0.1.2. The original is the reference; this copy is here for offline use.

What a finished piece of analysis must show, whatever the tool that produced the raw material. The standards below are those of the US Intelligence Community Directive 203, written for government analysts but adopted well beyond them because they are short, public and testable: a reviewer can take a report and check it against each line.

## The Intelligence Cycle
Intelligence is a process before it is a product. The classic cycle has six stages, and the last one is the one most often skipped.

1.  **Direction (planning):** the requirement. What question must be answered, for whom, by when, and within which legal and ethical limits. A collection that starts without a question collects everything and answers nothing.
2.  **Collection:** gathering the raw material from the sources the requirement points to. In OSINT this means searching, capturing and preserving, with the capture date and a hash of each item (see [OSINT Methodology](osint-methodology.md)).
3.  **Processing:** turning raw captures into something that can be analysed: exports parsed, text translated, duplicates removed, entities extracted, everything graded (see [Source Evaluation](source-evaluation.md)).
4.  **Analysis:** testing hypotheses against the evidence, with the techniques in [Analytic Techniques](analytic-techniques.md). This is where information becomes intelligence.
5.  **Dissemination:** the written product, delivered to the person who asked, in time to be used (see [Report Writing](report-writing.md)).
6.  **Feedback:** the customer says what was useful, what was missing and what has changed. Feedback becomes the next direction; without it the cycle is a line, and the next report repeats the mistakes of this one.

The UNODC manual draws the same idea at the analyst's desk as a loop: collate, draw a preliminary chart, infer, plan collection, collect, re-evaluate, revise, and only then conclude and write. Both pictures say the same thing: you go round more than once.

## The Five Analytic Standards
ICD 203 requires every analytic product to meet five standards. They are stated here in short; the directive itself is eight pages and worth reading whole.

**Objective:** perform the analysis with awareness of your own assumptions and reasoning, use techniques that reveal and mitigate bias, consider alternative perspectives and contrary information, and do not let a previous judgement hold when new information calls for a change.

**Independent of political consideration:** the assessment must not be distorted by, or shaped for, the preferences of an audience, an agenda or a policy. In a private investigation, read "client" for "policy": the answer is not the one the client hopes for.

**Timely:** disseminated in time to be acted on. A perfect report delivered after the decision is an archive document.

**Based on all available sources of intelligence information:** informed by all the relevant information available, with the critical gaps identified and addressed, and collection directed at them.

**Implements and exhibits analytic tradecraft standards:** the nine standards below.

## The Nine Analytic Tradecraft Standards
1.  **Properly describes quality and credibility of underlying sources, data and methodologies.** Every key judgement says what it rests on and how good that is. ICD 206 adds *source descriptors* and a *source summary statement*: a short paragraph on the strengths and weaknesses of the source base as a whole. In OSINT practice this is the 4 x 4 grade of every item and the "Sources" section of the report.
2.  **Properly expresses and explains uncertainties associated with major analytic judgements.** Two separate things: the *likelihood* of the event, and the analyst's *confidence* in the basis for saying so. The vocabulary and its rules are in [Estimative Language](estimative-language.md).
3.  **Properly distinguishes between underlying intelligence information and analysts' assumptions and judgements.** The reader must always be able to tell what was observed from what was concluded. State assumptions explicitly when they carry the argument or bridge a gap, and say what follows if they prove wrong.
4.  **Incorporates analysis of alternatives.** Identify and assess the plausible alternative hypotheses, especially when the stakes are high, the evidence is thin, or a low-probability event would have a large impact. Say which indicators would change the picture.
5.  **Demonstrates customer relevance and addresses implications.** Answer the question that was asked, and say what it means for the person who asked it.
6.  **Uses clear and logical argumentation.** A clear main message up front, judgements supported by information and reasoning, unambiguous language, internal consistency, and an honest account of the contrary evidence.
7.  **Explains change to or consistency of analytic judgements.** If this report changes what an earlier one said, say so and say why. Date and number your products so that the comparison is possible.
8.  **Makes accurate judgements and assessments.** Make the judgements that would be useful, including the difficult ones; do not avoid them to reduce the risk of being wrong. Precision is part of accuracy: the message the reader receives must be the one you meant to send.
9.  **Incorporates effective visual information where appropriate.** Charts, timelines, maps and link diagrams when they convey a relationship better than prose. A chart supports a written product; it never replaces it.

## Information, Intelligence and Evidence
Three words that are often used as synonyms and should not be:
- **Information** is knowledge in raw form: a post, a record, a screenshot, a statement.
- **Intelligence** is information that has been evaluated for its source and reliability and analysed in context. In the UNODC formula: *information + evaluation = intelligence*.
- **Evidence** is material that meets the rules of a court or a formal proceeding. OSINT can produce evidence, but only if collection, preservation and chain of custody were done to that standard from the start. The [Berkeley Protocol](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/publications/berkeley-protocol-on-digital-open-source-investigations/) sets that standard for digital open sources.

Analysis is not forensics. Digital forensics preserves and recovers data for proceedings; intelligence analysis evaluates information to support a decision. They share techniques, but mixing up their purposes leads to method errors: an "assessment" in a forensic report, or a chain-of-custody claim in an intelligence brief that was never collected that way.

## Further Reading
- **"ICD 203: Analytic Standards"** (ODNI, 2015, as amended) - The directive summarised on this page. [PDF](https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-203.pdf)
- **"ICD 206: Sourcing Requirements for Disseminated Analytic Products"** (ODNI) - Source descriptors, source summary statements and reference citations. [PDF](https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-206.pdf)
- **"Criminal Intelligence: Manual for Analysts"** (UNODC, 2011) - The intelligence process from the law-enforcement side: evaluation, analysis, link analysis, presentation. [PDF](https://www.unodc.org/documents/organized-crime/Law-Enforcement/Criminal_Intelligence_for_Analysts.pdf)
- **"Psychology of Intelligence Analysis"** by Richards J. Heuer Jr. (CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence, 1999) - Why the objectivity standard is hard to meet, and what to do about it. [CIA page](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/books-monographs/psychology-of-intelligence-analysis-2/) · [PDF](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Pyschology-of-Intelligence-Analysis.pdf)
- **"Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations"** (OHCHR and UC Berkeley Human Rights Center, 2020/2022) - The standard for collecting open-source material that may become evidence. [Human Rights Center](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/publications/berkeley-protocol-on-digital-open-source-investigations/) · [UN Digital Library](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3973652)
